chapters.name: Chapter 1: Capturing what you need to remember

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Voice reminders the moment you think of them
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Capture a reminder by voice before you forget it.
This lesson builds toward: The moment you think of something to do, you will capture a voice reminder that says what and when, using "every" for repeating ones, and mark it done when finished.
The best time to capture a reminder is the moment you think of it. Your phone's voice assistant (Siri on iPhone, Google Assistant or Gemini on Android) makes this quick: no typing, no searching for a pen.
Say: "Remind me to call the pharmacy tomorrow at 10 am." "Remind me to water the plants every Monday." "Remind me to take my umbrella when I leave home" works on some phones, which can remind you by location.
When the reminder appears, act on it or tap to snooze it. Mark it done when finished, so your list stays clear.
Step by step:
- Wake your voice assistant.
- Say "Remind me to..." with what and when.
- Use "every" for repeating reminders.
- When it appears, do it or snooze it.
- Mark it done.
Words to know:
- Snooze: to delay a reminder so it comes back a little later.
- Repeating reminder: a reminder that comes back on a schedule, like every Monday.
Try it now: Set two reminders by voice: one for tomorrow and one that repeats every week.
You can now capture one-time and repeating reminders by voice.

check.q: What does snoozing a reminder do?
options: Delays it a little so it comes back
check.why: Snooze delays the reminder a little; mark it done when you have finished.

check.q: You remember while cooking that you must call the bank tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Write it on a napkin later
Say to your phone: "Remind me to call the bank tomorrow at 10 am."
Call the bank now at night
check.why: Capture a reminder the moment you think of it, by voice, with what and when.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A notes list for things to remember
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep a "Things to remember" note on your phone and add to it by voice.
This lesson builds toward: Using Notes or Google Keep, you will keep a pinned "Things to remember" note and add to it by typing or voice, with no passwords or private numbers in it.
Some things are not tied to a time: the name of the new neighbor, the book a friend recommended, where you put the spare key. These belong in a note.
Open the Notes app (or Google Keep on many Android phones) and create a note called "Things to remember". Pin it to the top if your app allows. You can add to it by typing or by tapping the microphone on the keyboard and speaking.
Keep the note simple: one line per item, newest at the top. Never store passwords, bank numbers or Social Security numbers in a plain note.
Step by step:
- Open Notes or Google Keep.
- Create a note named "Things to remember".
- Pin it to the top if you can.
- Add items by typing or with the keyboard microphone.
- Keep private numbers out of it.
Words to know:
- Notes app: an app for writing and saving notes on your phone.
- Pin: to keep an item at the top of a list so it is easy to find.
Try it now: Create a "Things to remember" note and add three items, at least one by speaking with the keyboard microphone.
You can now keep a notes list for things you want to remember and add to it by voice.

check.q: What does pinning a note do?
options: Keeps it at the top of your notes
check.why: Pinning keeps your "Things to remember" note at the top where you can find it.

check.q: A friend recommends a book while you are out. Where does it go?
check.why: Things not tied to a time, like a book name, belong in your note.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Photos as memory aids
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use your camera to remember where things are and what they say.
This lesson builds toward: Given something you need to remember, such as where you parked, you will take a photo memory aid and find it again in your recent photos or an album, without photographing private cards or documents.
A quick photo can remember things for you. Take a picture of the parking spot sign or level number, the inside of the fridge before you shop, the label of a light bulb you need to replace, or the closed stove knobs before you leave.
To find these later, create an album called "Memory aids" in your photos app, or just look at your most recent photos. Delete them when you no longer need them.
Do not photograph private documents like bank cards or your Social Security card for this purpose; if your phone is lost, those photos could be misused.
Step by step:
- Take a quick photo of the thing to remember.
- Look at recent photos, or keep a "Memory aids" album.
- Delete memory photos when done.
- Do not photograph private cards or documents.
Words to know:
- Memory aid: anything that helps you remember, like a note, alarm or photo.
Try it now: Take one photo memory aid today, such as the inside of your fridge or where you parked. Find it again in your photos an hour later.
You can now use photos to remember where things are and what they say.

check.q: Why should you not keep a photo of your bank card as a memory aid?
options: If your phone is lost, the photo could be misused
The bank does not allow photos
check.why: Photos of private cards could be misused if the phone is lost.

check.q: You park on level 3 of a big garage. What is a quick way to remember?
options: Take a photo of the level sign
Write it in a text to a stranger
check.why: A quick photo of the parking sign remembers it for you.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Checklists made with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask AI for a short checklist for a task you do often.
This lesson builds toward: Given a task you do often, you will ask AI for a short checklist, edit it to fit your life and put it where you will see it, with no more than about eight simple items.
Checklists help everyone, from pilots to doctors. An AI assistant can make one for any routine task: leaving the house, getting ready for a trip, or the night before an appointment.
Ask: "Make me a short checklist for leaving the house: no more than eight items, in simple words." Then edit it to fit your home: "Add: check the back door. Remove: feed the cat."
Print it and tape it by the door, or save it in your Notes. A checklist only helps if it is where you will see it at the right moment.
Step by step:
- Choose a task you do often.
- Ask AI for a short checklist in simple words.
- Add or remove items to fit your life.
- Put it where you will see it at the right moment.
Words to know:
- Checklist: a list of steps you tick off one by one.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for a "before I leave the house" checklist of no more than eight items. Change it to fit your home, and print it or save it.
You can now make a personal checklist with AI and put it where it helps.

check.q: When does a checklist help most?
options: When it is saved where you never look
When it is where you will see it at the right moment
When only the AI can read it
check.why: A checklist only helps if you see it at the right moment, such as by the door.

check.q: The AI's checklist says "feed the cat" but you have no cat. What do you do?
options: Ask for a new list every day
Remove that item and add any you need
check.why: Edit the checklist so it fits your home.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Remembering what was said at appointments
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Capture the key points of an appointment or call and turn them into a clear summary.
This lesson builds toward: After an appointment or important call, you will turn your notes into a short summary and to-do list with AI help, with private details removed and anything unclear confirmed with the office.
It is easy to forget what the doctor, lawyer or repair person said. Bring a written list of questions, and write down the answers, or ask a family member to come along and take notes.
Afterward, type your rough notes into an AI assistant, without names, birth dates or account numbers, and ask: "Turn these notes into a short summary with a list of things I need to do." Save the summary in Notes.
If something is unclear, call the office to confirm. Many doctor's offices also post a visit summary in their patient portal. Some people ask whether they may record a visit on their phone; always ask permission first.
Step by step:
- Bring a list of questions and write down answers.
- Bring a family member if you can.
- Type rough notes into AI without private details.
- Ask for a summary and to-do list.
- Confirm anything unclear with the office.
Words to know:
- Summary: a short version of the main points.
- Patient portal: a website or app where your doctor's office shares visit notes and results.
Try it now: Write three rough notes from a recent call or appointment (leave out names and numbers). Ask an AI assistant to turn them into a short summary with a to-do list, and save it.
You can now capture and summarize what was said at an appointment or call.

options: A website or app where your doctor's office can share visit notes
check.why: Many doctor's offices post a visit summary in their patient portal.

check.q: You want to record what the doctor says on your phone. What do you do first?
check.why: Always ask permission before recording a visit.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: A daily memory routine
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put your memory tools together into a simple daily routine.
This lesson builds toward: Every day, you will follow a simple memory routine of morning and evening checks, and talk with your doctor about memory changes that worry you.
Tools work best as a habit. A simple daily routine: in the morning, look at today's reminders and calendar. During the day, capture reminders and notes the moment you think of them. Before bed, check tomorrow's reminders and your "Things to remember" note.
Keep things in the same places every day: keys, glasses and phone in one bowl by the door. A tracking tag on your keys (such as Apple AirTag or a Tile) can help you find them with your phone.
Be kind to yourself. Forgetting some things is normal. If you or your family notice memory changes that worry you, such as getting lost in familiar places or trouble with everyday tasks, talk with your doctor. MedlinePlus (medlineplus.gov) has trusted information about memory.
Step by step:
- Morning: check reminders and calendar.
- Daytime: capture reminders and notes right away.
- Evening: check tomorrow and your note.
- Keep keys, glasses and phone in one place.
- Talk to your doctor about worrying changes.
Words to know:
- Tracking tag: a small device on keys or a bag that your phone can find.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine)
Try it now: Final task: build your memory toolkit (two repeating voice reminders, a "Things to remember" note, one photo memory aid, and an AI-made "before I leave the house" checklist) and use it all for one full day with the morning and evening check.
You can now use reminders, notes, photos, checklists and AI summaries in a daily routine that supports your memory.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Voice reminders Fewer than two reminders, or they do not repeat. Two repeating reminders set by voice, each with what and when. Marked them done or snoozed them as they came up during the day. Things to remember note No note, or it holds passwords or private numbers. A "Things to remember" note with at least one item and no private numbers. The note is pinned and an item was added by voice. Photo memory aid No photo, or a photo of a private card or document. One useful photo memory aid, such as where you parked or a label. Saved in a "Memory aids" album and deleted when no longer needed. Leaving-the-house checklist No checklist, or it does not fit your home. A short AI checklist edited to fit your home and placed where you will see it. Used the checklist each time you left the house that day. Used for one full day The tools were set up but not used. Used the toolkit for one full day, with a morning and evening check. Can say which tool helped most and what to change. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a good evening memory habit?
options: Turn off your phone for a week
Check tomorrow's reminders and your "Things to remember" note
Write a new checklist every night
check.why: Before bed, check tomorrow's reminders and your note.

check.q: You keep losing your glasses around the house. What simple habit helps?
options: Keep keys, glasses and phone in one bowl by the door
check.why: Keeping things in the same place every day means you know where they are.
